title: I Built the Bullitt Mustang of My Childhood Dreams

body_markdown:
My dad was always into Mustangs. Growing up, he had a 1970 Shelby GT500 in the garage, and naturally, he showed me *Bullitt* when I was a kid. I thought it was the coolest movie I’d ever seen. We lived in Northern California, not far from San Francisco, so I was familiar with the city’s steep streets where the famous chase scene took place.


It definitely influenced me, and when I was older, I started looking for a 1967 or 1968 Mustang fastback that I could turn into a Bullitt replica. It took me a few years of searching, but in 2010, I found a 1968 S-code fastback that was as close to one of the movie cars as I was going to get. It was a factory Highland Green car with a 390-cubic-inch V-8 and a four-speed manual. Remarkably, it came from the same ordering district and San Jose assembly plant as the original movie cars. It had been purchased new from Lodi Ford in California and had stayed within the same family since 1968. On paper, I think I’m only the second owner.


*Welcome to the[Hagerty Movies and Cars Celebration](https://www.hagerty.com/media/magazine-features/welcome-to-the-hagerty-movies-and-cars-celebration/) , where we highlight and explore the relationship between[cars and the silver screen](https://www.hagerty.com/media/tags/movies-and-cars/) .*


Courtesy John Muhlenkamp


The main catch was that it needed a complete restoration. The original 390 was long gone, replaced by a 289, and the body was not in the best shape. With the help of a family friend who ran a Mustang restoration shop out of Grants Pass, Oregon, we performed a full rotisserie restoration. It wasn’t a fast process—it was 2020 by the time the car was finished.


Courtesy John Muhlenkamp


Courtesy John Muhlenkamp


During the restoration, I figured if I was going through all the effort, I might as well get the details right. I did a lot of research, which involved taking screenshots of the movie Mustang at different angles and joining online communities dedicated to Bullitt replicas. I had the reverse lights deleted to match the movie car and a fresh 390 built to put into the engine bay. One of the hardest parts to find was the driver’s-side mirror used in the movie. The original Ford part was removed in favor of an aftermarket one. Someone online identified exactly which mirror was used, so I started searching for one. When one finally appeared on eBay, I ended up in a bidding war with everyone else building a Bullitt replica and spent around $700 for it. It seemed crazy, but my car was already so close to the original that I felt like I had to have it.


Courtesy John Muhlenkamp


Now that it’s done, I love to take my Mustang to shows and for drives through the canyons here in Utah. Some people recognize it immediately as Steve McQueen’s Bullitt Mustang—others just see a beautiful green fastback. Either way, I’m so glad I was able to save this car and turn it into the Bullitt car I always dreamed about.
